lab_title: Structural Anatomy of the Human Heart and Dual-Loop Circulation
top_level_objectives: Identify and locate the four chambers of the heart (right atrium, right ventricle, left atrium, left ventricle) on a 3D model
Identify and locate the four cardiac valves (tricuspid, pulmonary, mitral/bicuspid, aortic) and explain their role in preventing backflow
Identify the major vessels entering and leaving the heart (superior and inferior vena cava, pulmonary arteries and veins, and aorta)
Trace the complete path of deoxygenated blood through the pulmonary circuit and oxygenated blood through the systemic circuit
Explain why the left ventricular myocardium is substantially thicker than the right ventricular myocardium in terms of functional demand

scenes.scene_name: External Orientation: The Heart in Context
scenes.brief_purpose: Anchor students spatially by placing a life-sized, semi-transparent AR heart model in the chest cavity of a human torso overlay, establishing anatomical position and directional terminology before any internal detail is introduced.
key_visuals: Life-sized human torso outline with ribcage landmarks visible in AR overlay
Whole heart model positioned slightly left of the midline, apex pointing inferiorly
Directional labels: superior, inferior, anterior, posterior, left, right
Pericardium shown as a translucent sac surrounding the heart
student_actions: Rotate the AR heart model 360 degrees to view it from anterior, posterior, and lateral perspectives
Tap directional labels to confirm understanding of anatomical position
Answer a brief orienting question: 'Which side of the thoracic cavity does the heart's apex point toward?' before advancing

scenes.scene_name: The Four Chambers: External Surface Landmarks
scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce the four chambers by highlighting their external boundaries on the intact heart, using surface grooves and color-coding to distinguish right-side (deoxygenated) from left-side (oxygenated) structures before cutting inside.
key_visuals: Color-coded heart surface: right chambers in blue-tinted overlay, left chambers in red-tinted overlay
Coronary sulcus and interventricular sulci highlighted as boundary landmarks
Animated chamber labels that fly in sequentially: right atrium, right ventricle, left atrium, left ventricle
Relative size comparison showing the left ventricle occupying a greater portion of the apex
student_actions: Tap each color-coded region to reveal its chamber name and a one-sentence functional summary
Drag a boundary line along the interventricular sulcus to confirm where the right and left ventricles divide
Complete a quick four-item matching exercise pairing each chamber to its general function (receiving vs. pumping; pulmonary vs. systemic)

scenes.scene_name: Inside the Heart: Chamber Walls and the Ventricular Difference
scenes.brief_purpose: Slice the heart open to reveal internal anatomy, with special emphasis on the stark difference in myocardial wall thickness between the two ventricles and the structure of the interventricular septum.
key_visuals: Coronal cross-section of the heart model with chamber interiors fully visible
Myocardial wall thickness rendered to scale: left ventricular wall ~3x thicker than right
Trabeculae carneae and papillary muscles visible inside both ventricles
Interventricular septum highlighted; fossa ovalis visible in interatrial septum
Side-by-side wall-thickness measurement callouts in millimeters (right ~3–5 mm, left ~10–15 mm)
student_actions: Use a virtual ruler tool to measure and compare wall thickness in the right vs. left ventricle
Tap the left ventricular wall to trigger an explanation of why higher systemic resistance demands greater myocardial mass
Answer a short-answer prompt: 'Why would a patient with long-standing high blood pressure develop an even thicker left ventricular wall?' to reinforce functional reasoning

scenes.scene_name: The Four Valves: Structure and Backflow Prevention
scenes.brief_purpose: Focus attention on each of the four cardiac valves in situ, illustrating how atrioventricular valves (tricuspid and mitral) and semilunar valves (pulmonary and aortic) differ structurally and how both types prevent retrograde blood flow during the cardiac cycle.
key_visuals: Isolated valve-plane cross-section ('valve level' view from above) showing all four valves simultaneously
Tricuspid valve with three cusps labeled and chordae tendineae connecting to papillary muscles
Bicuspid/mitral valve with two cusps and chordae tendineae highlighted
Pulmonary and aortic semilunar valves shown with three half-moon cusps each
Animated open/close cycle for each valve type, triggered separately
student_actions: Tap each valve to reveal its name, cusp count, and the specific moment in the cardiac cycle when it opens and closes
Trigger an animation showing a valve closing against attempted backflow, with a visual 'regurgitation blocked' indicator
Complete a drag-and-drop exercise placing each valve name at its correct anatomical position in the valve-plane view

scenes.scene_name: Major Vessels: Entry and Exit Points
scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce all major vessels connected to the heart, distinguishing veins (returning blood) from arteries (leaving blood), and establishing the physical entry/exit geography that will be traversed in the blood-flow trace.
key_visuals: External heart model with major vessels rendered and color-coded: blue for veins carrying deoxygenated blood, red for arteries carrying oxygenated blood (and blue for pulmonary arteries, red for pulmonary veins to highlight the exception)
Labels for: superior vena cava, inferior vena cava, pulmonary trunk and left/right pulmonary arteries, four pulmonary veins, and aorta
Arrows indicating direction of blood flow along each vessel
Pop-up callout noting the pulmonary artery/vein color convention reversal as a common point of confusion
student_actions: Tap each vessel to confirm its name, whether it carries oxygenated or deoxygenated blood, and which chamber it connects to
Recolor vessels in a 'blank' version of the model (drag a red or blue tag onto each vessel) to self-test before seeing the answer overlay
Answer a targeted question about why the pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood despite being arteries, reinforcing the definition of artery as 'away from the heart'

scenes.scene_name: Tracing Pulmonary Circulation: Right Heart to Lungs and Back
scenes.brief_purpose: Animate the complete pulmonary circuit as a guided blood-drop journey, letting students follow a bolus of deoxygenated blood from the body's return through the right side of the heart and out to the lungs, then back as oxygenated blood.
key_visuals: Animated blue blood-drop particle traveling: inferior/superior vena cava → right atrium → tricuspid valve → right ventricle → pulmonary valve → pulmonary arteries → lung capillary bed (simplified) → pulmonary veins
Each valve highlighted and labeled as the particle passes through it
Lung capillary bed shown in a simplified inset with O₂/CO₂ exchange indicated by color shift from blue to red
Step counter (e.g., 'Step 3 of 7') displayed throughout the animation
student_actions: Advance each step of the animation manually by tapping a 'Next' button, reinforcing sequential learning
At two pause points (before the tricuspid valve and before the pulmonary valve), identify which valve the blood will cross next before the animation reveals it
After the animation completes, reconstruct the pulmonary circuit path independently by arranging shuffled structure cards in the correct order

scenes.scene_name: Tracing Systemic Circulation: Left Heart to the Body and Back
scenes.brief_purpose: Animate the systemic circuit as a continuation of the previous scene, following the now-oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins through the left heart and out to the body, completing the dual-loop mental model.
key_visuals: Animated red blood-drop particle traveling: pulmonary veins → left atrium → mitral valve → left ventricle → aortic valve → aorta → simplified systemic capillary bed (body tissues) → superior/inferior vena cava
Left ventricular wall thickness prominently highlighted during the pumping step with a pressure callout (~120 mmHg systolic) vs. right ventricle (~25 mmHg), reinforcing the wall-thickness lesson
Aorta branching into major arteries shown schematically to convey the scope of the systemic circuit
Dual-loop summary diagram appearing at scene end showing both circuits side by side
student_actions: Again advance each step manually, predicting each valve before it is revealed
Tap the pressure callout labels to read an explanation connecting ventricular pressure to myocardial thickness

Complete a final integrative quiz: given a labeled blank heart diagram, draw or tap the complete path of a red blood cell from the inferior vena cava all the way back to the inferior vena cava, passing through both circuits

scenes.brief_purpose: Consolidate learning by connecting structural anatomy to two clinically relevant scenarios — mitral valve stenosis and left ventricular hypertrophy — and provide a full-lab review dashboard so students can gauge their mastery before leaving.
key_visuals: Split-screen comparison of a healthy mitral valve vs. a stenotic mitral valve with narrowed orifice highlighted
Split-screen comparison of normal vs. hypertrophied left ventricular wall with thickness measurements
Summary infographic mapping all 13 named structures (4 chambers, 4 valves, 5 major vessels) onto a clean heart diagram
Progress dashboard showing scores from each scene's embedded question
student_actions: Tap each clinical case card to read a two-sentence description of the condition and its direct anatomical cause
Revisit any scene marked incomplete or low-scoring from the progress dashboard
Complete a 10-question cumulative multiple-choice post-assessment covering chamber identification, valve function, vessel naming, and blood-flow sequence to earn lab completion credit
